extracted.intended_audience: the citizens (people of New York) considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for citizens and public-spirited readers on how to judge the work of the Constitutional Convention and the proposed federal Constitution, weighing its defects, compromises, and practical effects rather than insisting on theoretical perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and moderation in judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public measures should be investigated with a spirit of moderation essential to a just estimate of their tendency to advance or obstruct the public good; avoid predetermination to condemn or to patronize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not scan the plan with a predisposition to censure or with a predetermination to applaud; the papers are addressed to those who combine sincere zeal for the country with a temper favorable to a just estimate of means for promoting it. Make allowances for human fallibility when rejudging the convention's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presuming infallibility in critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who rejudge the fallible opinions of the convention should remember they themselves are but men and ought not to assume infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged errors of the convention, consider that critics are also subject to error; temper zeal with self-awareness about one's own fallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for novelty and limited precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The undertaking of framing a new federal government is novel; other confederacies provide warning of errors to avoid but do not point precisely to the correct model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that some defects are the result of lack of antecedent experience; understand some errors will not become apparent until practical trial. Value solutions that avoid known historical mistakes even if they cannot be ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance energy and stability against republican liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine requisite stability and energy in government with inviolable attention to liberty and the republican form; stability and energy are both essential but may pull in different directions from republican principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh trade-offs explicitly: republican liberty favors short durations, many hands, and dependence on the people; stability and energy favor longer continuance in office and concentrated execution (a single hand). Assess whether the Constitution achieves an appropriate compromise between these competing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully delineate federal vs State powers (expect ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marking the proper line of partition between general and State governments is exceedingly difficult; boundaries will be obscure because of complexity of objects, human conceptual limits, and limitations of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate ambiguous or equivocal provisions; allow for future liquidation of meaning through practice, discussion, and adjudication. Do not fault the plan solely for such unavoidable imprecision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept necessary compromises between large and small states
rubrics_metrics.description: The differing pretensions of larger and smaller States made compromise unavoidable; the convention likely sacrificed theoretical propriety to extraneous considerations to achieve agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging organization and distribution of powers, recognize that concessions were needed to secure unanimity and practical functioning; evaluate whether the compromises reasonably balance competing state interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test objections for coherence and proposed alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Many objections to the plan are incoherent or mutually inconsistent; objectors often disagree among themselves about what should be substituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing criticism, ask whether objectors deny the underlying problem, agree on the necessity of remedy, and propose a consistent and practicable alternative. Prefer the experiment recommended unanimously by competent advisers over disparate and conflicting alternatives from critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the new plan to the existing Confederation (comparative standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Constitution need not be perfect; it suffices that it is less imperfect than the existing Confederation, which has many comparable or worse defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reforms comparatively: ask whether the proposed system remedies the worst evils of the present system, rather than demanding unattainable perfection. Use the existing Confederation as a base-line comparator (e.g., powers of taxation, treaties, raising troops, bill of rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of multiplying experiments (risk of repeated discord)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming a second convention or repeatedly remodelling the plan risks reproducing the same discord and factional contests that afflicted the first convention; more tinkering does not guarantee a better result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the practical dangers of delay and renewed contentious deliberation; where the first convention produced a broadly acceptable remedy recommended by experienced and chosen representatives, the risk of further experimentation may outweigh potential theoretical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain discretionary emergency fiscal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Even unpopular impositions (e.g., poll taxes) should not be categorically excluded from federal power because there may be emergencies in which such measures become essential resources for the public weal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between the power to impose a tax and the likelihood it will be used; preserve discretionary fiscal tools for exceptional contingencies while judging proposed fiscal powers by their prudential use and institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design fiscal policy to use convenient revenue sources and protect poorer classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Union supplies revenue, it can prudently improve use of capital resources (like commercial imposts), reducing the need for more inconvenient methods, and should aim to make the luxury of the rich tributary to the public treasury to protect poorer classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating revenue provisions, consider whether the federal design will enable more efficient, less burdensome taxation overall and whether it creates incentives to protect the least wealthy by relying on consumption or luxury-based levies rather than regressive burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply symmetry test to objections (do not accept double standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many alleged dangers attributed to the proposed federal powers (indefinite taxation, raising troops, mixture of powers) exist under the Confederation already or in State governments; objectors should not treat a federal power as uniquely dangerous if the same or similar powers already function elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge criticisms by asking whether the same objection applies to the existing system; require objectors to justify why a federal exercise of a power is more dangerous than its current practice under the Confederation or States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presume conspiratorial systems of influence without evidence; align incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppositions of a system of corrupt influence in national councils are invidious and unnecessary; institutional design (e.g., attaching State officers to the Union by emoluments) can redirect local influences into national channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming malign motives; when considering alleged dangers of influence, also consider institutional mechanisms that can align local officers' interests with the national government and thereby mitigate feared abuses.
